{{Hatnote|1=Transcript of a 2025 video interview with former Decipher staffer [[Jason Winter]].}}
'''''Inside the Star Wars CCG: Secrets from Decipher''''' (23 November 2025) is an interview by the Imperial Remnant YouTube channel with [[Jason Winter]], who worked in Decipher's product development team from February 1996 to January 1998, answering rules questions, contributing to design and running tournaments. Participants: the Imperial Remnant host (interviewer), [[Jason Winter]].

Source: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aq_dwh8Ojys Inside the Star Wars CCG: Secrets from Decipher], Imperial Remnant, YouTube (23 November 2025).

''The text below is from the video's automatic captions, corrected for names and card titles; it has not yet been checked against the audio. Words that could not be made out are marked [unclear].''

== Transcript ==

Just to give people a quick catch-up: I had made a video on the Star Wars Customizable Card Game from Decipher, and you had commented on it, and you worked for Decipher at the time. '''[00:26] Jason Winter:''' Yeah, it's kind of amazing how much I can remember, it being now almost 30 years ago.

'''[00:39] Jason Winter:''' Yeah, this was basically my job right out of college. I had a little temp job for a few months in the town where I lived, and then I got out here to Virginia and did that.

But also there was Decipher, and they were showing off their Star Trek VCR game. I remember sitting playing that for a little bit. Then the next year, in '94, was when they were showing off the Star Trek CCG, and I spent basically the entire convention at their booth playing it, even occasionally running demos for other people once I learned how to play the game. I remember they had an actor there dressed up as a Klingon to play against you. That was pretty cool. And so that got me in with them a little bit. I got to know some of the people there, like you mentioned, Tom Braunlich and Rollie Tesh. They were the main creators of the Star Trek game, and later the Star Wars game.

'''[01:50] Jason Winter:''' So I continued a conversation with Tom throughout the rest of that year. At that point I was a junior in college; '94 was the summer between my junior and senior year. So that's when I again hung out there, helped them run the tournament a little bit, did some demos at the booth. So that's basically all it was back then. More so now: you can do stuff on the internet, do YouTube videos, Twitch streams or whatever, like this, for instance. It's the same sort of thing. I just hung out with them when I could at the Gen Cons and so forth, and I kept up with Tom. '''[12:55] Interviewer:''' Yeah, from what I read, it sounded like it was part of the plan the whole time, and it had a really generous plan going forward for how to release it without oversaturating your market or making your design team insane. And then it just went faster and faster and faster.

I don't remember when that launched exactly, but it also took a while. And I can remember: the motto of Decipher was "The Art of Great Games", and some fans called it "the art of late games".

'''[14:04] Interviewer:''' As a consumer, I was probably on that side. '''[14:37] Interviewer:''' Yeah, it's understandable, especially when each expansion pack came with add-on rules. The game still had to function.

'''[15:50] Interviewer:''' As far as creating the new cards—I don't know if you remember this much—was there a thing where you're like, okay, in Premiere this one card always kind of runs away, or if you have this specific combination it kind of dominates everything, we need to make a counter for it?

'''[16:04] Jason Winter:''' Yeah, there's always stuff like that in any CCG. One of the more controversial things we did: if you remember, back then the main characters—your Lukes, Vaders, whatever—were obviously very powerful, but they also had the small destiny number, which is like the die roll, the number in the corner, always like a one or something. Generally the rule was: the more useful the card, the lower its destiny number. So it was kind of supposed to be a bit of a counterbalance. Let's just say we weren't really great at designing counterbalance in games. Everyone packed their deck with Lukes and Vaders and whatever.

'''[16:33] Jason Winter:''' So one of the things we did—I think maybe around the ''Cloud City'' expansion, maybe ''Dagobah'', I don't remember—we did a card where, if I remember correctly, you flip over your top three cards, each player does, and looks at their destiny numbers, and the one with the lower total loses that much Force, or something like that. So I flip over Luke, Obi-Wan and Han; they're all ones. You flip over Stormtrooper number six three times, and he's got like a five or whatever. So you win 15 to three, and I lose 12 Force. Which is a sort of counter, but people didn't like that.

'''[17:07] Interviewer:''' Too strong?

'''[17:09] Jason Winter:''' No—you're making the main characters weak, in a way.

'''[17:13] Interviewer:''' Yeah, that's true. You pull the hero trinity and you lose massively to a mouse droid. [Laughter]

'''[17:18] Jason Winter:''' So that was a part of it. But another thing we had was, Sense and Alter were kind of our counterspells in that game. Sense countered an Interrupt; Alter countered an Effect; but they also countered each other. So that was another thing you'd have in decks; you had people playing like 20 of each or something like that. So we made a card that you could play as an Effect, and it was immune to Alter, so it couldn't be destroyed with that, and every time they played one of those, you could make them lose Force—I don't remember exactly what it was, but it was a specific Sense/Alter counteracting card. So we did try to do balance like that, because Decipher didn't want to do the Magic [approach]. They didn't want to ban cards; they didn't want to have deck limits. That was the more elegant way they wanted to do things. Warren was definitely a very artistic kind of guy and liked to have that kind of elegance in his games, and to separate them from how Magic worked. So that was the way they chose to go instead.

'''[18:15] Interviewer:''' A deck limit being, like, you can only have four of a card?

'''[18:18] Jason Winter:''' Right. The only limit we had is it still had to be 60 cards, because your deck was still your life force.

'''[18:24] Interviewer:''' Well, yeah, of course. You can't have one guy with a 300-card deck and one guy with 50.

'''[18:29] Jason Winter:''' Which reminds me—again, a bit of a tangent here—the deck sleeves, the plastic ones or the hard ones you put them in: one guy used to put his decks entirely in the hard sleeves, so his deck was like this tall. [Laughter]

'''[18:47] Interviewer:''' I remember the tournaments I played in, we could only use the soft plastic, and they had to be clear on both sides, because a lot of people were printing cards.

'''[18:53] Jason Winter:''' Oh, yeah.

'''[18:55] Interviewer:''' Trying to fake it. I remember that became a big thing in my very local area. Sorry, the animals are all over me. It's interesting hearing about the process of trying to balance the game, because, looking back—years later, of course—I remember it being difficult to play, but I don't ever remember there being what would be called the meta now, where, oh, if this guy puts 30 of this one card in the deck, there's nothing you could do; counter for absolutely everything, and then he just uses his remaining pile. But it sounds like that very much was the case, and I'm sure whatever balance you made to counter the first thing, in the next expansion you'd have to counter the one that you created. It's like introducing an invasive species every time.

'''[19:41] Jason Winter:''' Yeah. Well, one comment that Bill Martinson came up with—I think after Tom and Rollie kind of faded into the background, Bill was more the lead designer—his motto was "the threat is worse than the execution." So you could play a deck with 20 Senses and 20 Alters, but if you know that card is out there, that one card that's going to completely screw it over, you don't want to play with that, because your opponent might have it, and if they do, you basically lose. So even if the counters just existed—and we'd devote two or three cards per set to that sort of thing—it helps to balance that out, and people will be less likely to want to play those kinds of degenerate strategies.

'''[20:20] Interviewer:''' Okay, I see what you're saying. That makes sense. Just knowing that the strategy is a possibility, people would build in their own defenses to it preemptively.

'''[20:28] Jason Winter:''' Hopefully. Sometimes the cards were so powerful they didn't care: I'll take my chances. But that was a bit of a strategy we employed. "The threat is worse than the execution"—that's all I remember.

'''[20:44] Interviewer:''' I also like—maybe like your example of getting three heroes and then three generic background Stormtroopers, and the Stormtroopers win. Obviously that's not a great scenario for fans of the franchise, but I do like the attempts to say, okay, if Vader is this powerful, let's make something about him so you don't have 10 Vaders in your deck. I do like that effort.

'''[21:02] Jason Winter:''' Yeah. Well, the way we didn't have 10 Vaders in your deck was because they were so expensive, because they were also the rare ones as well—which is something we can blame Jerry Darcy for. Apparently he used to say that it was not his decision, full on, because he wasn't high-ranking or whatever, but I think Warren or someone said, "Hey, how should we do this? Should we make the Vader ultra rare?" And Jerry was like, "Sure." So that's how he described that it went. [Laughter] He agreed to it and they went with it. So, his fault.

'''[21:25] Interviewer:''' This might be jumping the gun, because I'm not sure what expansion it was in, but at one point I remember reading about kind of reprints but also kind of new cards, so instead of the card being Darth Vader, it was Vader, and then it became a lot more common.

'''[21:38] Jason Winter:''' Yeah, so that was the Vader in the two-player set. We made a two-player set pretty early on, which was meant to be a cheap entry point. I think it was like $20. So they're kind of equivalent, but they give you different strategies. You can always get that Aragorn in a starter deck, but if you want the cool strategy, you find the rare Aragorn. But if, like you said, a 13-year-old wanted Luke or Vader in his deck, he could buy that.

'''[25:19] Interviewer:''' It's interesting, the IP game. How many expansions did you stay around for?

'''[25:23] Jason Winter:''' So I was there from February '96 till January of '98. '''[53:36] Jason Winter:''' All right. Awesome. Take care.
